subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What are the 'Five Rights' of drug administration?
answer: 1. Right Patient: Verify with two identifiers (name, date of birth, hospital number). 2. Right Drug: Check medication label against order. 3. Right Dose: Verify calculation, check for high-alert medications. 4. Right Route: Confirm appropriate route (oral, IV, IM, etc.). 5. Right Time: Administer at scheduled time, check frequency. Additional 'Rights': Right documentation, Right indication, Right response, Right to refuse, Right education.
clinical_application: Critical safety check to prevent medication errors and adverse drug events

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: How do you calculate drug dosages for oral medications and injections?
answer: Basic formula: Desired dose ÷ Stock strength × Quantity = Amount to administer. Oral: D/H × Q. Injections: D/H × Q (where D=desired, H=have, Q=quantity/volume). IV flow rates: Total volume (ml) ÷ Time (hours) = ml/hr. Drops per minute: (Volume × Drop factor) ÷ Time in minutes. Pediatric dosing based on weight (mg/kg) or body surface area. Critical care: mcg/kg/min calculations.
clinical_application: Essential for accurate medication administration, preventing under/overdosing, especially in pediatrics and critical care

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: Describe the procedure for intramuscular injection
answer: Sites: Ventrogluteal (preferred), dorsogluteal, deltoid, vastus lateralis. Procedure: 1. Verify order, perform hand hygiene. 2. Gather equipment: syringe, needle (22-25G), medication, alcohol swab, gauze. 3. Identify patient, explain procedure. 4. Prepare medication using aseptic technique. 5. Position patient appropriately. 6. Identify landmark, clean site in circular motion. 7. Insert needle at 90° angle quickly. 8. Aspirate (controversial; check facility policy). 9. Inject slowly (10 sec/ml). 10. Withdraw, apply pressure. 11. Activate safety device, dispose properly. 12. Document.
clinical_application: Common route for vaccines, antibiotics, hormones; requires proper technique to prevent injury and ensure absorption

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What is the procedure for intravenous injection?
answer: 1. Verify order, perform hand hygiene. 2. Gather equipment: syringe with prepared medication, tourniquet, alcohol swab, gauze, tape, IV cannula if not in situ. 3. Identify patient, explain procedure. 4. Select vein (cephalic, basilic, median cubital). 5. Apply tourniquet. 6. Clean site. 7. Insert cannula at 15-30° angle, look for flashback. 8. Advance, remove stylet, attach extension set/flush. 9. Secure with dressing. 10. Administer medication slowly per guidelines (push rate). 11. Observe for infiltration, extravasation, adverse reactions. 12. Flush after administration. 13. Document.
clinical_application: Critical for emergency medications, chemotherapy, and drugs requiring rapid onset; high risk for complications

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: How do you administer eye drops correctly?
answer: 1. Verify order, perform hand hygiene. 2. Gather medication, gloves, tissues. 3. Identify patient, explain procedure. 4. Position patient sitting or lying with head tilted back. 5. Remove contact lenses if present. 6. Remove cap, avoid touching dropper tip. 7. Gently pull down lower lid to create conjunctival sac. 8. Ask patient to look up. 9. Instill prescribed number of drops into sac, not directly on cornea. 10. Release lid, ask patient to close eyes gently. 11. Apply gentle pressure to inner canthus (nasolacrimal occlusion) for 1-2 minutes to reduce systemic absorption. 12. Wait 5 minutes between different eye drops. 13. Document.
clinical_application: Common for glaucoma, infections, allergies; proper technique ensures effectiveness and reduces systemic effects

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What are the principles of aseptic technique?
answer: 1. Only sterile items touch sterile areas. 2. Sterile surfaces contact only sterile surfaces. 3. Keep sterile fields dry (moisture wicks bacteria). 4. Consider edges of sterile field as contaminated. 5. Never turn back on sterile field. 6. Keep sterile items above waist level (in view). 7. Avoid talking, coughing, sneezing over sterile field. 8. Minimize air movement. 9. Use sterile gloves when touching sterile items. 10. Open sterile packages away from sterile field first. 11. Maintain sterile field at all times.
clinical_application: Essential for wound care, catheter insertion, surgery, and any procedure breaching sterile body areas

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: Differentiate between sterilization, disinfection, and decontamination
answer: Sterilization: Complete elimination of all microorganisms including spores. Methods: Autoclaving (steam under pressure), dry heat, ethylene oxide gas, radiation. Used for surgical instruments, implants. Disinfection: Eliminates pathogens but not necessarily all spores. High-level: Kills all except some spores (boiling, chemical sterilants). Intermediate: Kills TB, viruses, bacteria (alcohol, bleach). Low-level: Kills some bacteria/viruses (quaternary ammonium). Decontamination: Process reducing microorganisms to safe level (cleaning with detergent).
clinical_application: Guides proper processing of equipment based on Spaulding classification (critical, semi-critical, non-critical items)

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: Describe the technique for wound dressing
answer: 1. Assess wound, gather appropriate supplies. 2. Perform hand hygiene, don gloves. 3. Position patient, provide privacy. 4. Remove old dressing, observe drainage. 5. Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene. 6. Open sterile dressing tray using aseptic technique. 7. Don sterile gloves. 8. Clean wound: From cleanest to dirtiest area, using circular motion from center outward. Use new swab for each stroke. 9. Apply prescribed ointment/medication. 10. Place sterile dressing over wound. 11. Secure with tape. 12. Dispose of contaminated materials properly. 13. Document wound appearance, drainage, patient response.
clinical_application: Promotes healing, prevents infection, allows wound assessment, and provides patient comfort

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: How do you remove sutures?
answer: 1. Verify order, assess wound healing (typically 7-14 days post-op). 2. Perform hand hygiene, gather supplies: sterile suture removal kit (forceps, scissors), gloves, antiseptic swabs, dressing. 3. Explain procedure, position patient. 4. Clean wound with antiseptic. 5. Using sterile forceps, gently lift suture knot. 6. Cut suture close to skin on one side (avoid cutting visible part above skin). 7. Gently pull suture out with forceps toward wound line. 8. Count sutures removed. 9. Assess wound for dehiscence. 10. Apply sterile dressing if needed. 11. Document number removed, wound appearance, patient tolerance.
clinical_application: Removes non-absorbable sutures after wound healing; incorrect technique can cause wound dehiscence

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What are the risks associated with unsafe injection practices?
answer: 1. Transmission of bloodborne pathogens: HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C. 2. Bacterial infections: Abscesses, sepsis. 3. Nerve damage: Needle injury to peripheral nerves. 4. Tissue necrosis from incorrect injection. 5. Allergic reactions. 6. Medication errors. 7. Needlestick injuries to healthcare workers. 8. Toxic effects from incorrect medication/dose. 9. Abscess formation from contaminated equipment. 10. Psychological trauma. WHO estimates 1.3 million deaths annually from unsafe injections.
clinical_application: Understanding risks motivates adherence to safe injection practices and proper sharps disposal

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What are the WHO recommendations for injection safety?
answer: 1. Use sterile equipment for each injection. 2. Prevent contamination of injection equipment. 3. Use aseptic technique. 4. Prevent needle stick injuries (safety-engineered devices). 5. Safe sharps disposal: puncture-proof containers, no recapping. 6. Avoid unnecessary injections. 7. Use single-dose vials when possible. 8. Proper hand hygiene. 9. Appropriate skin preparation. 10. Vaccinate healthcare workers against HBV. 11. Monitor and evaluate injection practices. 12. Educate patients and providers. One needle, one syringe, only one time.
clinical_application: Standardized protocols to prevent injection-associated infections and injuries

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: How are healthcare wastes classified?
answer: 1. Infectious waste: Contaminated with blood, body fluids, cultures. 2. Pathological waste: Human tissues, organs, body parts, fetuses. 3. Sharps: Needles, scalpels, broken glass. 4. Pharmaceutical waste: Expired, unused drugs. 5. Cytotoxic waste: Chemotherapy agents. 6. Chemical waste: Laboratory reagents, disinfectants. 7. Radioactive waste: Nuclear medicine, radiotherapy. 8. General waste: Non-hazardous (similar to household). Color coding: Yellow (infectious), Red (sharps), Black (general), Brown (chemical), etc.
clinical_application: Proper segregation reduces environmental impact, prevents injuries, and ensures regulatory compliance

subject: Foundation of Nursing II
question: What are the key steps in healthcare waste management?
answer: 1. Segregation: Separate at point of generation using color-coded containers. 2. Collection: Regular collection in designated containers. 3. Storage: Secure, labeled area with limited access. 4. Transport: Safe internal and external transport. 5. Treatment: Autoclaving, incineration, chemical treatment. 6. Disposal: Landfill for treated waste. 7. Monitoring: Track waste streams, maintain records. 8. Training: Educate all healthcare workers. 9. Personal protective equipment. 10. Emergency procedures for spills.
clinical_application: Systematic approach to protect healthcare workers, public, and environment from hazardous waste
